sources.name: Flex Association - App-Based Industry Impact: California (one-page fact sheet)
sources.contains: Industry-lobby one-pager (Public First analysis of Flex member rideshare + delivery data for 2022; Morning Consult 2023 survey). Statewide counts of 'active app-based workers' (rideshare and delivery combined, 'active' undefined), transactions, economic impact. No LA breakdown, no delivery-vs-rideshare split, no vehicle type.
headline_datapoints: 870,000 active app-based workers in California (2022 data)
7.3M app-based workers in the U.S.; 4.3B app-based transactions (2022)

sources.name: National Equity Atlas / UC Berkeley Labor Center / USC ERI - 'Prop 22 Depresses Wages and Deepens Inequities for California Workers' (Prop 22 pay study)
sources.contains: Post-Prop 22 earnings study of California rideshare and delivery drivers (SF and LA), net hourly earnings after expenses, healthcare-stipend qualification analysis. Methodology page at https://www.nationalequityatlas.org/about/our-data/prop-22-pay-study-report-methodology (fetch returned HTTP 403). Also hosted by USC ERI: https://dornsife.usc.edu/eri/publications/prop-22-depresses-wages-and-deepens-inequities-for-california-workers/
sources.granularity: state, with SF and LA metro samples
headline_datapoints: Average earnings after expenses, not including tips: $7.12/hr for ride-hailing drivers, $5.93/hr for delivery workers (2024 study, per search summary)
Drivers who qualify for the health care stipend could earn the equivalent of ~$6.75/hr; majority of drivers could not qualify for the stipend (per search summary)
Press coverage: California app drivers make 'as little as $7.63 an hour' after expenses; SF and LA drivers earned less than drivers in three non-California cities (SF Examiner, May 2024)

sources.name: UC Berkeley Labor Center / CWED - 'Gig Passenger and Delivery Driver Pay in Five Metro Areas'
sources.contains: Trip-level earnings analysis for gig passenger and delivery drivers in Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, SF Bay Area, Seattle; uses driver-submitted trip data. Press release: https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/release-gig-passenger-and-delivery-driver-pay-in-five-metro-areas/
sources.granularity: metro (includes Los Angeles and SF Bay)
headline_datapoints: 52,370 trips by 1,088 drivers across Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco Bay and Seattle metros, January 2022 (per search summary)
Drivers often earned less than the local minimum wage after expenses such as gas (per search summary)

sources.name: UCLA Labor Center / IRLE - 'More Than a Gig: A Survey of Ride-hailing Drivers in Los Angeles'
sources.contains: First comprehensive survey of TNC (Uber/Lyft) drivers in LA County: hours, income dependence, vehicle costs, organizing preferences. RIDE-HAIL only, not food delivery; no e-bike/moped data. Summary: https://irle.ucla.edu/2018/05/31/new-ucla-report-finds-driving-is-more-than-a-casual-gig-for-la-ride-hailing-drivers/
headline_datapoints: 260 surveys and 8 in-depth interviews with TNC drivers in LA County (2018)
About half of drivers work full-time hours; for 1 in 2 drivers driving is their sole job; 2 of 3 rely on driving as main income source (2018)

sources.name: UCLA Labor Center - 'Worker Ownership, COVID-19, and the Future of the Gig Economy'
sources.contains: UCLA Labor Center report on gig economy during COVID and cooperative models; surfaced in search only, contents not verified. Possible LA gig-worker context; unlikely to contain courier counts or vehicle splits.

sources.name: NYC DCWP - 'A Minimum Pay Rate for App-Based Restaurant Delivery Workers in NYC' (study + proposed rule)
sources.contains: DCWP study (Nov 2022) using platform-submitted trip data plus worker survey: weekly-active worker count, demographics, pay before/after expenses, transport mode, per-hour expense allowance for e-bike workers. Hearing/report page: https://www.nyc.gov/site/dca/workers/Delivery-Worker-Public-Hearing-Minimum-Pay-Rate.page ; 2025 rule update: https://rules.cityofnewyork.us/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/DCWP-NOA-Rules-Relating-to-Contracted-Delivery-Workers.pdf ; full-rate-in-effect release (Apr 2025): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dca/news/009-25/mayor-adams-full-minimum-pay-rate-app-based-restaurant-delivery-workers-now-in
sources.year: study Nov 2022; rule adopted June 2023; full rate April 2025
headline_datapoints: More than 60,000 New Yorkers perform deliveries for a restaurant app on any given week; 58% aged 18-34, 75% male, 91% non-white or Hispanic (2022)
Average $14.18/hr before expenses (half app pay, half tips); $11.12/hr after expenses with tips; $4.03/hr after expenses without tips (2022)

Search summary claims ~44% of food delivery workers used cars and 56% used non-car modes, principally e-bikes, and DCWP added $2.26/hr as average e-bike expense - UNVERIFIED against primary report; the car share looks high for NYC and must be checked before use as a mode-split benchmark

sources.name: Seattle Office of Labor Standards - First App-Based Worker Minimum Payment Ordinance (SMC 8.37) Data Report
sources.contains: Administrative data submitted by the five largest network companies (restaurant, grocery/retail, package delivery) covering Jan 15 2024 - Jun 29 2025: covered worker counts, offers, pay per engaged hour, mileage. Announcement: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/WASEATTLE/bulletins/414169a ; research page: https://www.seattle.gov/laborstandards/ordinances/app-based-worker-ordinances/app-based-worker-research ; UW Harry Bridges Center update (May 2026): https://labor.washington.edu/news/2026-05/research-update-app-based-worker-minimum-pay-ordinance
headline_datapoints: 92,801 workers covered over the first 18 months across the five largest network companies; ~15 million offers (2024-2025)
Average network company payment per engaged hour $30.12 after subtracting mileage expenses during engaged time (2024-2025)
Note: 92,801 is a cumulative 18-month count of anyone who worked, NOT daily-active; includes grocery and package delivery, not only restaurant couriers

sources.contains: 2025 peer-reviewed study of California ridehailing and courier drivers' transportation/labor challenges; potentially includes vehicle-type data for couriers. Fetch returned HTTP 403; abstract not read. Check for open-access preprint (e.g., UC eScholarship / UC ITS).

sources.contains: Compilation/synthesis of worker surveys on app-based work (national, includes California studies). Advocacy organization; useful as an index of primary surveys rather than as a data source.

sources.name: Uber Newsroom - 'First Independent Survey Shows 4 out of 5 California Drivers with Uber Are Happy Prop 22 Passed'
sources.contains: Platform-commissioned driver satisfaction survey post-Prop 22; company-funded, no courier counts or vehicle mode expected.

sources.name: LA City Clerk Council File Management System (search portal for any delivery-worker pay motions)
sources.contains: Where any LA City Council motion on app-based delivery worker minimum pay would be filed. One targeted web search found NO such motion or ordinance for 2025; LA results were all hotel/airport ($30/hr by 2028) and general minimum wage ordinances. Not yet searched directly.
headline_datapoints: No LA City ordinance or council motion specific to app-based delivery worker minimum pay surfaced in this pass (as of 2026-09-06 search)

gaps: No public source found that counts daily-active or weekly-active food-delivery couriers in Los Angeles City/County, let alone DTLA + Koreatown; unlike NYC and Seattle, LA has no delivery-worker pay ordinance generating platform-submitted administrative data.

No LA-specific survey with a vehicle-mode split (car / motorcycle-scooter / e-bike / bicycle) for delivery couriers was found; the UCLA Labor Center LA work found is 2018 ride-hail (car) only. Vehicle-mode split remains the biggest unknown for tasks 1 and 4.

Prop 22 healthcare-stipend enrollment counts: only qualitative findings (majority cannot qualify) surfaced; no absolute enrollment numbers by county were found. These would be held by platforms or the state and may not be public.

California EDD and BLS gig-work surveys (e.g., BLS Contingent Worker Supplement, EDD labor market data) were not searched in this pass due to the call budget; expect national/state granularity only, no LA courier counts.

Primary pages for the two most relevant studies (National Equity Atlas Prop 22 methodology; ScienceDirect 2025 CA courier paper) returned 403; UCSC SF delivery-worker study URL returned 404. Sample sizes and LA/SF splits are therefore unverified and must be pulled in the full-research pass (try PDF mirrors, USC ERI, UC eScholarship).

NYC and Seattle counts are weekly-active (NYC) or cumulative 18-month (Seattle) and cover grocery/package delivery in Seattle; converting them to a daily-active per-capita or per-restaurant ratio requires the restaurant/population denominators from other modalities and a separate active-vs-registered adjustment.

The Flex Association '870,000 active app-based workers in California' figure is industry-funded, combines rideshare and delivery, does not define 'active', and cannot be apportioned to LA without an external allocation key.
No academic or government source addresses theft/security exposure of courier vehicles in DTLA/Skid Row (task 6); that will need police/crime modalities.
must_ask_hmp: Actual vehicle-mode mix of HMP's 1,000+ SF customers (e-bike vs 28-35 mph vs 40-50 mph e-moped vs e-motorcycle) and which platform(s) each rider works for - no public LA/SF survey substitutes for this.

Daily-active share of the 1,000+ sold vehicles and of the ~300 battery renters / ~100 whole-vehicle renters (how many riders actually deliver on a given day/week), needed to calibrate any NYC/Seattle-style active-worker ratio.

Rider earnings data HMP collects at the 'confirm earnings' step before purchase (hourly/weekly gross, hours, platform) - a far better LA unit-economics input than the Prop 22 study's statewide $5.93/hr net figure.
Home ZIP codes vs delivery-zone ZIP codes of SF riders, to estimate how far riders will travel to a depot (critical for whether a Skid-Row-edge hub can serve Koreatown/Westlake riders).
Churn, theft/loss incidents, and repair frequency per vehicle class in SF, to set LA replacement-fleet and security parameters.
Any existing LA customer or inbound-inquiry data (web orders shipped to LA ZIPs, LA phone inquiries) that would give a direct read on LA demand independent of public studies.
surprises: Seattle's ordinance data report shows 92,801 distinct covered workers over 18 months in a city of roughly three-quarters of a million residents - the pool of people who EVER deliver is an order of magnitude larger than plausible daily-active counts; any ratio-based LA estimate must explicitly separate registered/ever-active from daily-active.

The search summary of the NYC DCWP study attributes ~44% car use to NYC food-delivery workers, which conflicts with the common belief that NYC couriers are overwhelmingly on e-bikes; if it holds up against the primary report, LA (a far more car-oriented city) could have a much larger car share than the CONTEXT's e-bike/moped framing assumes - verify before use.

The 2024 Berkeley/USC/National Equity Atlas Prop 22 study puts California delivery workers at $5.93/hr net of expenses excluding tips (vs $7.12 for ride-hail), i.e., delivery riders' ability to carry a weekly rental plus battery subscription is thinner than ride-hail-based intuition suggests.

Los Angeles has no delivery-worker minimum-pay ordinance or equivalent data-reporting requirement (none surfaced for 2025), so unlike NYC/Seattle there is no administrative dataset to anchor LA courier counts; the LA sizing will have to be triangulated rather than read off a government report.
